performers: Skidmore College Orchestra, per the Free Music Archive and Internet Archive; not named on the Commons page
question: What happens to the walking theme when it is slowed into a lament?
intro: The walking theme returns changed into a lament, beneath a quiet tremolo. In Lamm’s piano text it starts on F♯, moves chromatically, and later settles on a fixed high F♯. Here the visitor stops looking at the pictures and speaks to the dead. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

sections.label: The theme as a hushed lament

cues.title: The Promenade as a ghost
cues.text: The Promenade theme returns as a hushed lament, with ethereal strings and delicate woodwinds. F♯ is among the three strongest pitch classes in all 23 five-second windows; the count shows the note is always present, not that it is held or where it lies.
cues.evidence: Ethereal strings and delicate woodwinds, the Promenade theme: Philharmonia guide (Joanna Wyld). The report’s top three pitch classes include F♯ in every one of the 23 windows from 0:00 to 1:50; the first three windows read F, F♯, E and F♯, F, E. Pitch-class presence cannot show a continuously held note or its register. In Lamm’s piano text (Mutopia, promenade-6.ly) the upper tremolo begins on F♯ and then changes chromatically, with a fixed high F♯ tremolo as a later backdrop. The local key reading is F♯ minor, which here confirms a dominant of B minor and is not used as proof.

cues.title: Notes in the margin
cues.text: Mussorgsky pencilled on the manuscript: “Latin text: with the dead in a dead language”, then added that the creative spirit of the dead Hartmann leads him towards the skulls, which “begin to glow softly”.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (movement 8) quotes both pencilled notes; Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note gives them in another translation. Related edge: hartmann-pictures--mussorgsky-pictures-1874. The note sits near the quietest early window (−11.9 dB at 0:30).

cues.title: The sound opens out
cues.text: The strongest boundary of the movement comes at about 0:58, and the level climbs from about −10 dB to −5.4 dB at 1:00, among its loudest windows. After it the statements are fuller; the lament is now heard by a larger orchestra.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 0:58 (novelty 1.00); relative level −10.5 dB (0:55), −5.4 dB (1:00) and −4.4 dB (1:10), the loudest windows. The report does not identify which instruments join.

cues.title: Observer and observed
cues.text: At the Catacombs the Promenade stops being a mere link and becomes part of the picture itself. In this movement the line between the visitor and what he looks at disappears.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article, section “Movements”: the turn at the Catacombs, where the Promenade theme becomes an integral element of Cum mortuis and the line between observer and observed vanishes. The note sits in a quieter stretch (−7 to −12 dB, 1:15–1:35).

cues.title: A last swell, then a quiet B major
cues.text: Near 1:45 the sound swells once more, reaching −6.8 dB, before the final window at 1:50 falls to −15 dB. The score ends on a B major chord under a fermata: a major close to a minor lament. No timestamp is claimed for it.
cues.evidence: Relative level −8.8 dB (1:40), −6.8 dB (1:45; one of the loudest windows) and −15.0 dB (1:50, the quietest window); onsets per second 1.0, 0.6, 0.4. The final B–D♯–F♯ chords with a fermata are in Lamm’s piano text (Mutopia, promenade-6.ly); the report cannot time the final chord, so the ending is described only as a broad closing region.

transitions.title: The lament grows to full volume
transitions.from: The theme as a hushed lament
transitions.how: Near 0:58 the level climbs about five decibels in five seconds to reach one of the movement’s loudest windows at 1:00, and the statements that follow are fuller. The report cannot tell which instruments join. In the piano text the later bars lie over a fixed high F♯ tremolo, but the recording cannot be aligned to those bars, so the match is left open.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 0:58 (novelty 1.00); relative level −10.5 dB (0:55) to −5.4 dB (1:00); the report’s top-three pitch classes include F♯ in all 23 windows, which is presence and not a held note. The fixed high F♯ tremolo as the later backdrop is in Lamm’s piano text (Mutopia, promenade-6.ly); where it begins in this recording is not aligned.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (1:52; this file is 1:50), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
